about: Preview only (npm run dev:example): ten made-up teammates answer the survey of the demo meeting "Late submission policy", and "summary" is the In-meeting part an agent (OpenClaw) would write from their answers 30 minutes before the meeting. It shows what the In-meeting tab looks like with a real AI summary. Nothing here is real.

grace-period.reason: Most late uploads I saw were upload timeouts a few minutes after midnight. One hour covers that without inviting people to start late.
15 minutes is enough for upload hiccups. An hour just moves the deadline to 1 am.

A deadline is a deadline. After two weeks, any grace period becomes the real deadline.

summary.intro_md: **Goal:** one late-submission rule for the rest of the semester, to announce in next week's lecture.

grace-period.consensus_md: **Half of the team wants a 1-hour grace period** (5 of 10). Two prefer 15 minutes, two prefer 24 hours, and one wants none. Almost everyone who explained their choice agrees that the rule must be **the same for every group** and announced clearly.
key_points: Most late uploads are technical (upload timeouts a few minutes after the deadline).
Concern: a long grace period quietly becomes the real deadline.
A 24-hour window could replace most extension emails (2 people).

penalty.short: After the grace period: deduction or case by case?
penalty.consensus_md: **No clear majority.** A 10% deduction per day and a case-by-case decision by the head TA have the most support (4 of 9 each). Three would accept late work but grade it pass/fail; two would not accept it at all. One person skipped the question.
key_points: Several people chose more than one option, so a combination is possible.
Only 2 of 9 want to refuse late work completely.
penalty.disagreement_md: The split is **a fixed rule versus judgement**. Those for a 10% deduction want something predictable for students; those for case by case want room for illness and emergencies. A combination (10% per day, which the head TA can waive) might work for both sides.
